topics.title: 47.1 Mutexes
topics.summary: A mutex coordinates exclusive ownership. A thread acquires it before accessing protected mutable state and releases it afterward. Correct use establishes both exclusion and the ordering needed to observe prior protected updates. A mutex protects a rule about state , not a particular memory address by magic. If another function accesses the same state without the mutex, the rule is broken. Keep the state private behind an interface where practical so that callers cannot bypass the protection accidentally.

topics.title: 47.2 Lock
topics.summary: Locking obtains exclusive ownership, potentially waiting while another thread owns the mutex. A lock acquisition is therefore a possible blocking point. Avoid assuming that a short critical section always makes acquisition immediate. Use RAII ownership such as std::lock_guard or std::unique_lock in C++ to tie release to scope. Manual lock/unlock pairs are vulnerable to early returns and exceptions. unique_lock is appropriate when the code needs controlled unlocking or condition-variable waiting.

topics.title: 47.3 Unlock
topics.summary: Unlocking releases ownership and permits another participant to acquire the mutex. All protected invariants should hold at this boundary. An exception that leaves partially updated state must either restore the invariant or make failure state explicit before release. Do not unlock a mutex from a thread that does not own it under the ordinary mutex contract. Do not retain references to mutable internal data and then access them after unlocking unless a separate lifetime and synchronization rule permits it.

topics.title: 47.4 Critical sections
topics.summary: The critical section contains the operations that must be observed together. For an account transfer, checking funds and updating both balances belong to one logical transaction. Protecting only the final store leaves a check-then-act race. Keep sections focused. Expensive computation can often be performed on a snapshot outside the lock, but the result may need validation when applied. Releasing the lock does not freeze the state that was inspected earlier.

topics.title: 47.5 Protected state
topics.summary: Related fields should be grouped under a clear protection policy. A queue’s storage, head, tail, count, and closure flag may form one invariant. Protecting each field with an unrelated lock can expose combinations that never represented a valid queue state. Document the policy near the data definition. For example: “All reads and writes of these balances require mutex_ ; their sum remains constant.” Such a statement is more useful than a vague comment saying “thread-safe class.”

topics.title: 47.6 Lock invariants
topics.summary: A lock invariant describes what is true whenever protected state is available to another owner. Temporary internal states can exist while the lock is held, but they must not escape through callbacks, unlocked references, or exceptions. An invariant also guides tests. Verify conservation laws, bounds, and relationships, not only whether threads finish. A program that never crashes can still lose items, duplicate work, or violate accounting constraints.

topics.title: 47.7 Coarse-grained locking
topics.summary: Coarse-grained locking uses one lock for a broad region or related state group. It is often easier to prove correct and avoids many lock-order problems. For modest contention, its simplicity can outweigh theoretical parallelism lost inside the critical section. The cost appears when unrelated operations serialize behind the same mutex. Measure contention before splitting the design. A clear coarse-grained implementation provides a valuable correctness baseline for later optimization.

topics.title: 47.8 Fine-grained locking
topics.summary: Fine-grained locking divides protection among smaller state regions. It can allow independent operations to proceed concurrently but adds ownership, ordering, and lifecycle complexity. Operations spanning regions may need several locks. A finer design must define a consistent acquisition order or use a deadlock-avoiding multi-lock facility. More locks can also increase memory use, cache traffic, and maintenance cost. Fine-grained is a tradeoff, not a synonym for faster.

topics.title: Worked example — Preserve a conservation invariant
topics.summary: The ledger below starts with 1000 units on the left and zero on the right. Four workers each move 100 units, one at a time. One mutex protects both balances, and every transfer preserves their sum. Companion listing: ch47/ledger.cpp The expected output is left=600 right=400 . No transfer can observe the half-updated pair because all protected access uses the same mutex. Returning a copied snapshot keeps callers from retaining a reference that would bypass the lock after the function returns. The arithmetic is bounded by the initial total, so the example’s unsigned additions cannot exceed 1000. A general financial or inventory system would need explicit numeric range and domain rules rather than assuming those bounds remain true for arbitrary inputs.

The mutex is useful because the protected-state rule is consistent across all access paths.

topics.summary: One global mutex around an entire table is easy to reason about but serializes unrelated operations. One mutex per bucket can allow independent buckets to proceed concurrently but complicates operations touching multiple buckets. Fine-grained locking trades simpler contention behavior for more complicated ordering and invariant management.
